body.text: Will it rain in Mbale this afternoon? Will a boda boda be waiting at the stage? We often talk about how likely things are. Probability gives a number to how likely an event is, so we can compare chances and make better decisions.
Words we use in probability

items: An experiment is an action whose result we cannot be sure of, such as tossing a coin or rolling a die.
An outcome is one possible result, such as getting a head.
The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. For one die it is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An event is one outcome or a group of outcomes, such as getting an even number.
Random means that nobody can control or predict the result, and each outcome has its fair chance.
Probability is a number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an event is.

body.text: On the probability scale, 0 means impossible and 1 means certain. An even chance, like a head on a fair coin, is 1/2 or 0.5. When all outcomes are equally likely, we use this rule:

body.latex: P(A) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{total number of outcomes}}
body.speech: the probability of A equals the number of outcomes in A divided by the total number of outcomes

body.text: The probability space
A probability space, also called a possibility space, is a table or list of every outcome of an experiment. It is most useful when an experiment has two parts, such as rolling two dice.

For two dice, draw a 6 by 6 grid. Write 1 to 6 along the top for the first die and 1 to 6 down the side for the second die. In each cell, write the sum of the two numbers. There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes.

body.title: Rolling two dice
steps: Find the probability that the sum of two fair dice is 7.
The grid has 36 outcomes in total.
The pairs that add up to 7 are (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2) and (6, 1). That is 6 outcomes.
No other sum appears 6 times in the grid, so 7 is the most likely total.

body.text: Experimental and theoretical probability
Theoretical probability is worked out by reasoning, as we did with the dice. Experimental probability comes from repeating an experiment many times and counting. It is also called relative frequency.

body.latex: \text{experimental probability} = \frac{\text{number of times the event happened}}{\text{number of trials}}
body.speech: experimental probability equals the number of times the event happened divided by the number of trials

body.text: Suppose Opio tosses a coin 100 times and gets 46 heads. The experimental probability of a head is 46/100 = 0.46. The theoretical probability is 0.5. As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theoretical value.
Real-life data works in the same way. If a boda boda stage records that 18 of its last 60 trips went to Nakawa, the probability that the next trip goes to Nakawa is about 18/60 = 0.3.

body.title: Toss a coin 100 times
body.text: In pairs, take a coin and agree which side is the head. Toss it 100 times and record each result as H or T. After every 10 tosses, work out the proportion of heads so far. Plot the proportion of heads against the number of tosses and describe what happens. Then toss two coins together 100 times and count how often you get 0, 1 or 2 heads. Compare your counts with the possibility space HH, HT, TH, TT.
Mutually exclusive and independent events
Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen at the same time. Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 with one die are mutually exclusive. For mutually exclusive events, add the probabilities.

body.speech: the probability of A or B equals the probability of A plus the probability of B

body.text: Two events are independent if one does not change the probability of the other. Tossing a coin and rolling a die are independent. For independent events, multiply the probabilities.

body.speech: the probability of A and B equals the probability of A times the probability of B

body.text: Tree diagrams

A tree diagram shows each stage of an experiment as a set of branches. Write the probability on each branch. Multiply along a path to find the probability of that path. When more than one path gives the event you want, add their probabilities.

body.title: Rain on two days in Gulu
steps: On any day in April, the probability of rain in Gulu is 0.6. Assume the days are independent. Find the probability that it rains on exactly one of two days.
Day 1 has two branches: Rain (0.6) and No rain (0.4). From each of these, Day 2 has the same two branches.
These two paths are mutually exclusive, so add them: 0.24 + 0.24 = 0.48.
Check: the four paths give 0.36, 0.24, 0.24 and 0.16, which add up to 1.

body.text: Venn diagrams
A Venn diagram shows sets as overlapping circles inside a rectangle. You met them in Senior 2 set theory. The numbers in each region help you find probabilities.

body.title: Games in a class in Jinja
steps: In a class of 40 learners, 22 play football, 15 play netball and 6 play both.
Draw two overlapping circles, F and N, inside a rectangle. Write 6 in the overlap.
Learners in at least one circle: 16 + 6 + 9 = 31. Neither: 40 − 31 = 9, written outside the circles.
P(a learner chosen at random plays neither game) = 9/40.
P(the learner plays exactly one game) = (16 + 9)/40 = 25/40 = 5/8.

body.text: In one class, 30 learners each belong to one or two of three clubs. The Arts Club list has 15 names, the Science Club 12 and the Mathematics Club 13. How could you find how many learners are in two clubs without knowing which clubs they joined?

Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. Add probabilities for mutually exclusive events and multiply them for independent events. Possibility spaces, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams help you organise outcomes.
